prose.en: In order to throw the opponent, it is first necessary to make the opponent's posture unstable. Making the posture unstable in this way is called "kuzusu" (breaking balance). To break the opponent's balance you make use of the opponent's strength and movement, or push or pull with your own strength. The basic forms of kuzushi are the kuzushi in the eight directions.

Getting into a posture from which it is easy to throw, while breaking the opponent's posture, is called "tai-sabaki". The basic forms of tai-sabaki include "mae-sabaki" (forward body movement), "ushiro-sabaki" (rearward body movement), "mae-mawari-sabaki" (forward turning body movement) and "ushiro-mawari-sabaki" (rearward turning body movement).
③ Break balance on the spot → break balance while moving → break balance using tai-sabaki
Breaking balance from a stationary state

Decide who is tori and who is uke. From a stationary state, using a half-step movement, tori breaks uke's balance in the eight directions. Next, tori uses forward, backward, left and right movement to break uke's balance. Then tori uses tai-sabaki to break uke's balance. Through this practice, students learn the difference between a broken posture and a stable posture.

Breaking balance using tai-sabaki Point: At first, have students get the feel of kuzushi with the opponent in a stationary posture; then have them become able to break balance using movement and tai-sabaki. Point: If you try to break the opponent's balance by pulling or pushing with the arms alone, your own posture also collapses and you cannot break their balance well. Break the opponent's balance with the movement of the whole body while keeping your own posture, for example by using advancing and retreating movement forwards, backwards, left and right, and tai-sabaki. At this time, the ma-ai (distance) from the opponent is also important.

Working in pairs, tori breaks uke's balance in various directions and has uke take the side breakfall. At this stage the pair do not yet take a full grip: tori grips both of uke's wrists or the underside of the sleeves, so that the breakfall can be practised on both the left and the right.

Depending on how one is thrown, there are cases where the side breakfall is taken with the arm only ①, and cases where it is taken using the arm and the legs ②. Generally, when thrown backward or sideways the legs come up and it becomes a side breakfall with the arm only ①; when thrown forward, with the centrifugal force of the rotation added, it becomes a side breakfall using the arm and the legs ②.

Once students are used to it, uke raises the right leg and develops the feel of taking the breakfall backward with the left foot as a support. This is effective as an introduction to reaping techniques such as ō-soto-gari (major outer reap).
Make uke's right foot the support for the rotation.

Tori breaks uke's balance forward with the forward turning body movement and, using the rotational power of the body, throws uke forward. At this time, make uke's right foot the support for the rotation.

By repeating this kind of paired practice, tori and uke together can become proficient in a feel in which the movement, kuzushi (breaking balance), tai-sabaki and ukemi (breakfalls) needed when throwing are all unified.

第４章　技能指導の要点
⑶　崩しと体さばき
　○崩し
　相手を投げるためには、まず相手の体
勢を不安定にすることが必要です。この
不安定な体勢にすることを「崩す」とい
います。相手を崩すには、相手の力や動
作を利用したり、自分の力で押したり、
引いたりします。基本的な崩しには八方
向の崩しがあります。
　○体さばき
　相手の姿勢を崩しながら、投げやすい体勢になることを「体さばき」といいます。基本的な体さ
ばきには、「前さばき」「後ろさばき」「前回りさばき」「後ろ回りさばき」などがあります。
